intro: Bit manipulation techniques exploit the binary representation of integers to enumerate subsets, encode DP states compactly, and reason about XOR as a vector space over GF(2). Two of the most powerful and frequently-tested ideas are bitmask subset enumeration (culminating in Sum-over-Subsets DP and bitmask DP over states) and the XOR linear basis, which turns 'what XOR values are reachable' questions into linear algebra. Mastering both unlocks a large class of Codeforces 1700-2200 problems that look intractable under brute force.

subtopics.name: Subset Enumeration via Bitmasks (incl. Sum over Subsets DP)
subtopics.theory:
A set of n elements has 2^n subsets, and when n is small (typically n <= 20-22) you can afford to index an array by bitmask and treat each integer in [0, 2^n) as 'the subset whose i-th bit tells you whether element i is included.' This turns subset-DP problems into ordinary array DP problems where the array has 2^n entries. Two closely related but distinct patterns fall out of this: (1) bitmask DP over states, where dp[mask][extra] represents the best way to reach a state described by mask, and (2) Sum over Subsets (SOS) DP, which for every mask computes an aggregate (sum, OR, max, count) over all 2^n submasks of mask simultaneously in O(2^n * n) instead of the naive O(3^n) you'd get by enumerating (mask, submask) pairs directly.

The SOS DP trick is the following: to compute g[mask] = aggregate over all submasks s of f[s], iterate over bit positions b = 0..n-1, and for every mask that has bit b set, merge in the value of g[mask with bit b cleared] (which by induction already reflects the correct aggregate restricted to submasks that agree with mask on bits 0..b). After processing all n bits, g[mask] correctly aggregates over every one of the 2^popcount(mask) submasks of mask, even though you only ever did O(2^n * n) work. The reason this works is that flipping bit b independently is idempotent across masks, so processing bits one at a time and accumulating results is equivalent to a DP whose states are 'submask restricted to the first b bits' — a classic instance of the divide-and-conquer-by-bit-position idea that also underlies digit DP.

A second major pattern is DP over 'profile' bitmasks representing the state of a row, frontier, or partial assignment — for example broken-profile DP on grids (where a bitmask encodes which cells in the current frontier are already filled) or the Traveling Salesman Problem, where dp[mask][last] represents the minimum cost to have visited exactly the set of cities in mask, ending at city 'last'. This turns an O(n!) brute-force search into an O(2^n * n^2) DP, which is a huge win for n up to about 18-20 (2^20 * 400 ~ 4*10^8, borderline feasible; n <= 15 is comfortably fast).

The unifying insight across both patterns is that a bitmask is just a dense, O(1)-comparable, O(1)-updatable encoding of a small set, so any DP whose state naturally involves 'which subset of a small universe has been used/visited/included' can be array-indexed by that bitmask instead of using a hash map or explicit set structure.
subtopics.recognition: Look for: (a) small n (usually n <= 20-22) with a question about subsets, arrangements, or 'assign/visit every element exactly once'; (b) a request to precompute, for every subset, some aggregate over all its sub-subsets (sum/count/OR/AND over submasks) — this is the SOS DP signature; (c) grid or sequence DP where the state needs to remember 'which of a small set of slots/cities/items are already used', which screams dp[mask][...].
subtopics.complexity: Bitmask DP over states: typically O(2^n * n) to O(2^n * n^2) time, O(2^n) to O(2^n * n) space. SOS DP: O(2^n * n) time and O(2^n) space, versus the naive O(3^n) direct-enumeration alternative.

examples.title: Sum over Subsets (SOS) DP — core template
examples.problem: You are given an integer n (1 <= n <= 20) and an array f of size 2^n, indexed by bitmask, where f[mask] is given for every mask from 0 to 2^n - 1. For every mask, compute g[mask] = sum of f[s] over all submasks s of mask (a submask s of mask satisfies (s AND mask) == s, i.e. every set bit of s is also set in mask; mask itself and 0 both count as submasks). Print g[0], g[1], ..., g[2^n - 1] separated by spaces.
examples.approach: Initialize g as a copy of f. Then for each bit position b from 0 to n-1, sweep over all masks; whenever mask has bit b set, add g[mask with bit b cleared] into g[mask]. After processing bit b, g[mask] correctly equals the sum of f over all submasks of mask that only vary from mask in bits 0..b (an invariant provable by induction on b). After all n bits are processed, g[mask] is the full sum over all submasks of mask. This costs O(2^n * n) total work, versus O(3^n) if you enumerated every (mask, submask) pair directly (since a mask with k set bits has 2^k submasks, and summing 2^popcount(mask) over all masks gives exactly 3^n).

examples.title: Compatible Pair Search via SOS 'exists' DP
examples.problem: You are given n integers a[1..n] (0 <= a[i] < 2^B, here B = 4 so values are 0..15) and an integer B. For each index i (1-indexed), find any value a[j] (1 <= j <= n, j may equal i) such that a[i] AND a[j] = 0 (their binary representations share no common set bit), and print that value; if no such value exists among the array elements, print -1 instead. Print n answers separated by spaces.
examples.approach: a[i] AND a[j] = 0 exactly when a[j]'s set bits are a subset of the complement of a[i]'s bits, i.e. a[j] is a submask of comp = FULL_MASK XOR a[i] (FULL_MASK = 2^B - 1). So precompute, for every possible mask in [0, 2^B), a representative value rep[mask] that IS a submask of mask and DOES appear in the array (or -1 if none does). This is exactly SOS DP but with 'OR of existence' instead of 'sum': initialize rep[v] = v for every value v present in the array, then for each bit b, whenever a mask has bit b set and rep[mask] is still unset, pull rep[mask with bit b cleared] up into rep[mask]. Finally, for each a[i], the answer is rep[FULL_MASK XOR a[i]]. This runs in O(2^B * B + n) instead of O(n^2).

examples.title: Traveling Salesman via Bitmask DP over Visited-City Subsets
examples.problem: Given n cities (2 <= n <= 15) and an n x n matrix cost[i][j] giving the cost of traveling directly from city i to city j (cost[i][i] = 0), find the minimum total cost of a tour that starts at city 0, visits every other city exactly once, and returns to city 0.
examples.approach: Let dp[mask][i] be the minimum cost to have started at city 0, visited exactly the set of cities in mask (mask always includes bit 0), and currently be standing at city i (bit i set in mask). Base case dp[{0}][0] = 0. Transition: from dp[mask][i], for every city j not yet in mask, update dp[mask | (1<<j)][j] = min(dp[mask | (1<<j)][j], dp[mask][i] + cost[i][j]). After filling the table for all 2^n masks, the answer is min over i != 0 of dp[FULL][i] + cost[i][0], where FULL = (1<<n) - 1 (all cities visited). This is O(2^n * n^2) time and O(2^n * n) space, tractable for n up to ~15-18, versus the O(n!) brute force over permutations.

subtopics.name: XOR Properties & Linear Basis
subtopics.theory:
XOR has three properties that make it behave like addition in a vector space over the field GF(2): it is associative, commutative, and every element is its own inverse (x XOR x = 0). This means the set of all values reachable by XOR-ing together some subset of a given multiset of integers forms a linear subspace of GF(2)^k (thinking of each integer as a k-bit vector), and standard linear algebra — specifically Gaussian elimination — applies directly. The 'XOR linear basis' (also called a 'binary basis' or 'XOR basis') of an array a[1..n] is a maximal linearly independent subset (over GF(2)) built so that basis[b] is either 0 or a value whose highest set bit is exactly bit b.

You build the basis incrementally: for each new number x, walk its bits from the highest possible bit down to bit 0; at each set bit b of the current (possibly already reduced) x, if basis[b] is empty, x becomes the new basis[b] and you stop processing this number; if basis[b] is already occupied, XOR it into x (this eliminates bit b from x, exactly like a row-reduction step) and continue to lower bits. If x reduces all the way to 0, it contributed nothing new (it was already in the span of the existing basis) and no insertion happens. After processing all n numbers, the nonzero entries of basis[] form a linearly independent set that spans exactly the same subspace as the original array under XOR.

Once you have the basis, two classic questions become easy: (1) the MAXIMUM XOR achievable by any subset is found greedily — starting from result = 0, for each basis vector from the highest bit down to the lowest, XOR it into result if doing so INCREASES result (this greedy works because higher bits dominate lower ones in integer comparison, and each basis[b] is the only remaining vector that can toggle bit b without disturbing bits above b); (2) the NUMBER OF DISTINCT XOR VALUES achievable by any subset of the array is exactly 2^r, where r is the rank (number of nonzero vectors) of the basis — this is just the size of the subspace spanned by an r-dimensional basis over GF(2).

A separate but equally important XOR tool is the binary trie (a trie built over the bits of each number, most-significant-bit first). It supports, for a fixed query value x and a dynamic set of numbers, finding the number in the set that maximizes (or minimizes) x XOR y in O(B) time (B = number of bits), by greedily walking down the trie choosing, at each level, the child bit that disagrees with the corresponding bit of x whenever that child exists (this maximizes the resulting bit at that position). Binary tries generalize to support insertion, deletion (via per-node reference counts), and range-bounded variants (by inserting elements in sorted order and processing queries offline).
subtopics.recognition: Look for: (a) any question about 'maximum/minimum XOR of a subset', 'is XOR value V achievable', or 'how many distinct subset-XOR values exist' — these are linear-basis questions; (b) any question about 'maximum/minimum XOR of a PAIR (or of x with an element from a dynamic set)' — these are binary-trie questions; (c) the array size can be large (n up to 10^5-10^6) but values are bounded (fit in ~20-60 bits), which rules out O(2^n) brute force and points to the O(n * bits) linear-algebra or trie approach.
subtopics.complexity: Building an XOR linear basis: O(n * B) time where B is the bit-width (e.g. 60 for 64-bit values), O(B) space for the basis. Binary trie: O(B) per insertion/query, O(n * B) total space in the worst case.

examples.title: Maximum XOR Subset via Linear Basis
examples.problem: Given an array of n integers (1 <= n <= 2*10^5, 1 <= a[i] < 2^60), find the maximum possible value of the XOR of the elements of some non-empty subset (a single element counts as a valid subset).
examples.approach: Build the XOR linear basis of the array as described above: for each a[i], reduce it against the current basis (XOR-ing away any bit that already has a basis vector) and, if the result is nonzero, insert it at its highest remaining bit. Once the basis is built, greedily construct the maximum achievable XOR: starting from res = 0, iterate basis vectors from the highest bit position down to the lowest, and whenever XOR-ing the basis vector into res would make res strictly larger, do it. This greedy is optimal because each basis vector's leading bit is unique and not shared by any lower-indexed basis vector, so setting a higher bit whenever possible can never later be beaten by any combination of lower bits.

examples.title: Counting Distinct Subset XOR Values
examples.problem: Given an array of n integers (1 <= n <= 2*10^5, 0 <= a[i] < 2^60), count how many distinct values can be formed by taking the XOR of the elements of some subset (including the empty subset, whose XOR is defined as 0).
examples.approach: Build the XOR linear basis exactly as in the maximum-XOR problem, and let r be its rank (the number of nonzero basis vectors actually inserted). The set of all subset-XOR values is precisely the linear span of the basis, which — because the basis vectors are linearly independent over GF(2) — has exactly 2^r distinct elements (every one of the 2^r combinations of 'include basis vector b or not' yields a different XOR value, since basis vectors have distinct leading bits so no two different combinations can collide). The answer is therefore simply 2^r; no explicit enumeration of subsets or basis combinations is needed.

examples.title: Maximum XOR Pair via Binary Trie
examples.problem: Given an array of n integers (2 <= n <= 10^5, 0 <= a[i] < 2^20), find the maximum value of a[i] XOR a[j] over all pairs of indices i < j.
examples.approach: Maintain a binary trie over the 20-bit representation of the numbers seen so far (most significant bit first). Process the array left to right; before inserting a[i], if the trie already contains at least one previously-inserted number, query it: walk down the trie from the root, and at each level try to go to the child representing the bit OPPOSITE to the current bit of a[i] (since that maximizes the XOR contribution at that bit position); if that child doesn't exist, fall back to the child matching a[i]'s bit. The bits collected along this walk form the maximum XOR achievable between a[i] and any previously inserted element. Track the running maximum over all i, then insert a[i] into the trie and continue. Because each element is compared only against elements inserted strictly before it, every pair (i, j) with i < j is considered exactly once, giving O(n * 20) total time.
